q.s: Rafael wants to have $5,000 in 5 years. His account pays 12% interest compounded quarterly. About how much must he deposit today?
q.r: $2,768. Present value equals future value / (1 + r)^n. With quarterly compounding, the rate per period is 12% / 4 = 3% and there are 5 x 4 = 20 periods, so PV = $5,000 / 1.03^20 = about $2,768. The $2,837 answer assumes annual compounding, $3,125 assumes simple interest, and $2,000 subtracts 60% from the goal. More frequent compounding means less must be deposited today.
w: This simply takes 60% (12% x 5 years) off the $5,000 goal, which is not how discounting works; present value divides by 1.03 raised to the 20th power.
This assumes interest is compounded once a year ($5,000 / 1.12^5), but the account compounds quarterly, at 3% for 20 periods.
This uses simple interest ($5,000 / 1.60) and ignores interest earning interest; with quarterly compounding, Rafael needs to deposit less.

q.pt: Calculate the time value of money
q.s: Wren invests $1,000 at 8% interest compounded annually. What will the investment be worth at the end of 3 years?
q.r: $1,259.71. Future value equals present value x (1 + r)^n: $1,000 x 1.08^3 = $1,259.71. Compounding means each year's interest also earns interest. The $1,240.00 answer uses simple interest ($80 x 3 years) and ignores compounding. The $1,080.00 answer covers only one year. The $1,360.49 answer compounds for four years instead of three.
w: This covers only one year of interest ($1,000 x 1.08), but Wren's money grows for three years.
This uses simple interest ($80 a year for 3 years) and ignores that each year's interest also earns interest when it is compounded.
This compounds for four years ($1,000 x 1.08^4) instead of the three years in the question.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of convergence/consolidation in the finance industry
q.s: In the strict legal sense, what happens when two financial firms combine through a consolidation?
o: both original companies end and a new company is formed.
each company continues operating as a separate firm.
one company buys a small minority stake in the other.
one company absorbs the other and keeps operating under its own name.
q.r: Both original companies end and a new company is formed. In a consolidation, two or more firms combine and give up their separate identities, creating an entirely new organization. In a merger, by contrast, one company absorbs the other and survives. Companies that continue operating separately have not combined at all, and buying a minority stake is an investment, not a consolidation. Consolidation reduces the number of firms in the finance industry.
w: If each company keeps operating as a separate firm, the two have not combined at all, so no consolidation has taken place.
Buying a small minority stake is an investment in another firm, not a combination of two companies into one.
When one company absorbs the other and keeps its own name, that is a merger, while a consolidation ends both firms and creates a new one.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of convergence/consolidation in the finance industry
q.s: Meridian Financial offers checking accounts, insurance policies, mutual funds and brokerage services, all drawing on a single pool of capital. Meridian is best described as a(n)
q.r: Fully integrated financial services provider. Convergence in the finance industry has allowed one company to offer banking, insurance and investment services together, using one capital base, so customers can meet many financial needs in one place. A single-line insurer sells only one kind of insurance. A community savings and loan association focuses on local deposits and home loans. An independent brokerage firm buys and sells securities but does not offer banking or insurance.
w: An independent brokerage buys and sells securities for clients, but Meridian also offers checking accounts and insurance, which goes well beyond brokerage.
A single-line insurer sells just one kind of insurance, while Meridian offers banking, mutual funds and brokerage as well.
A community savings and loan focuses on local deposits and home loans, not the insurance, mutual funds and brokerage services Meridian offers.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of convergence/consolidation in the finance industry
q.s: Financial firms often merge or consolidate in hopes of
o: achieving economies of scale and higher earnings.
reducing their total assets and customers.
becoming exempt from federal and state banking regulations.
q.r: Achieving economies of scale and higher earnings. Combining financial firms lets them spread fixed costs such as technology and compliance over a larger customer base, cut duplicate operations and cross-sell more products, all of which can raise earnings. Combined firms usually offer more products, not fewer. Mergers do not exempt firms from regulation; large firms often face closer oversight. Growth in assets and customers, not a reduction, is the usual goal.
w: Combined firms usually offer more products so they can cross-sell to a larger customer base, not fewer products.
Firms merge to grow, so the usual goal is more assets and more customers, not fewer of each.
Merging does not exempt firms from banking rules, and larger combined firms often face closer oversight from regulators.

q.pt: Describe types of costs used in managerial accounting (e.g., direct cost, indirect cost, sunk cost, differential cost, etc.)
q.s: Which of the following is an indirect cost for a company that makes several kinds of office furniture:
o: Fabric used to cover a specific sofa
Wages of the worker who assembles chairs
Lumber used to build a specific desk
q.r: Insurance on the factory building. An indirect cost is shared by several products or departments and cannot be traced to any single one, so it must be allocated. Insurance on the factory protects the production of every product made there. Lumber for a desk, wages of a chair assembler and fabric for a sofa can each be traced to a specific product, which makes them direct costs.
w: Fabric used to cover a specific sofa can be traced directly to that one product, which makes it a direct cost.
The wages of a worker who only assembles chairs can be traced to the chairs, so they are a direct cost of that product.
Lumber used to build a specific desk can be traced straight to that desk, which makes it a direct cost rather than a shared one.

q.pt: Describe types of costs used in managerial accounting (e.g., direct cost, indirect cost, sunk cost, differential cost, etc.)
q.s: Last year, Teagan's firm spent $40,000 on a study of new accounting software. As the manager now decides whether to buy the software, she ignores the $40,000 because it is a(n)
q.r: Sunk cost. A sunk cost has already been spent and cannot be recovered no matter which choice is made, so it is not relevant to future decisions. The manager should compare only the future costs and benefits of buying or not buying the software. A differential cost is the difference in cost between alternatives. A variable cost changes with activity level. An opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative given up.
w: A variable cost rises and falls with activity level, while the $40,000 study was a one-time cost already paid in the past.
A differential cost is a future cost that differs between choices, but the $40,000 was spent last year and stays the same whatever the manager decides.
An opportunity cost is the value of the next-best option given up, not money that was already spent last year on a study.

q.pt: Describe types of costs used in managerial accounting (e.g., direct cost, indirect cost, sunk cost, differential cost, etc.)
q.s: An insurance agency is choosing between two office software packages. Package A would cost $18,000, and Package B would cost $25,500. The $7,500 difference between the two options is a(n)
q.r: Differential cost. A differential cost, also called an incremental cost, is the difference in total cost between two alternatives, here $25,500 - $18,000 = $7,500. Managers weigh it against any differences in benefits to choose the better option. A sunk cost was spent in the past and cannot be recovered. An indirect cost is shared among products or departments. A fixed cost stays the same regardless of activity level.
w: An indirect cost is shared among several products or departments, not the gap in price between two software packages being compared.
A sunk cost has already been spent and cannot be recovered, while the $7,500 is a future cost that depends on which package the agency picks.
Fixed overhead is a shared cost that stays the same as activity changes, not the difference in price between two choices.

q.pt: Describe marginal analysis techniques and applications
q.s: Under marginal analysis, a business should keep increasing production as long as
o: marginal revenue is at least equal to marginal cost.
total revenue is greater than the firm's total fixed costs.
marginal cost is greater than marginal revenue.
average cost per unit continues to rise.
q.r: Marginal revenue is at least equal to marginal cost. Marginal revenue is the added revenue from selling one more unit, and marginal cost is the added cost of producing it. As long as each additional unit brings in at least as much as it costs, producing it does not reduce profit, and profit is greatest where the two are equal. Comparing total revenue with fixed costs or watching average cost does not show whether one more unit pays. When marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue, profit falls.
w: Covering fixed costs with total revenue says nothing about whether the next unit adds more revenue than cost, which is what marginal analysis checks.
When marginal cost is greater than marginal revenue, each extra unit lowers profit, so the business should stop increasing production.
Rising average cost per unit is a warning sign, not a reason to keep producing, and it does not show whether one more unit pays for itself.

q.pt: Describe marginal analysis techniques and applications
q.s: Fairhaven Savings Bank is deciding whether adding a new youth savings account will pay off. What should the bank's managers do?
o: Add it if fees cover the research already spent on it
Compare the account's added revenue with its added cost
Base the decision on the bank's total costs last year
Add it because several competing banks offer a similar account
q.r: Compare the account's added revenue with its added cost. This is marginal analysis: managers estimate the additional revenue the new product would bring and the additional cost of offering it, and add it if the added revenue is at least as great. Copying competitors ignores the bank's own costs and revenue. Last year's total costs are historical and do not isolate the new product. Research already spent is a sunk cost and is irrelevant.
w: The research money is already spent and cannot be recovered, so it is a sunk cost that should not decide whether to add the account.
Last year's total costs are historical and cover the whole bank, so they do not show the added cost and added revenue of the new account.
Copying competitors ignores whether the new account's added revenue would actually be greater than its added cost for Fairhaven.

q.pt: Describe techniques used to analyze customer financial information
q.s: Before approving a car loan for Dana, a credit analyst at Ridgeway Credit Union reviews whether Dana has paid her past bills on time. Which factor is the analyst examining?
q.r: Payment history. Payment history is the record of whether a borrower has paid past debts and bills on time, and it is the factor lenders weigh most heavily when judging willingness to repay. The debt-to-income ratio compares monthly debt payments with income. Collateral is property pledged to secure a loan. Length of employment shows job stability but says nothing about how bills were paid.
w: The debt-to-income ratio compares monthly debt payments with income, which measures Dana's ability to pay, not whether past bills were paid on time.
Collateral is property, such as the car itself, pledged to secure the loan, not Dana's record of paying past bills on time.
Length of employment shows job stability, but it does not reveal whether Dana paid past bills on time.

q.pt: Describe techniques used to analyze customer financial information
q.s: Bayside Marine Supply has current assets of $240,000, including $90,000 of inventory, and current liabilities of $100,000. What is its acid-test ratio?
q.r: 1.5. The acid-test, or quick, ratio removes inventory from current assets because inventory may be hard to turn into cash quickly: ($240,000 − $90,000) ÷ $100,000 = 1.5. A result of 2.4 is the current ratio, which keeps inventory in. A result of 0.9 divides only the inventory by current liabilities, and 3.3 incorrectly adds inventory to current assets instead of subtracting it.
w: This is the current ratio ($240,000 / $100,000), which keeps inventory in; the acid-test ratio subtracts the $90,000 of inventory first.
This divides only the $90,000 of inventory by current liabilities, but the acid-test ratio uses current assets minus inventory.
This adds inventory to current assets ($330,000 / $100,000), when the acid-test ratio is supposed to remove it.

q.pt: Describe techniques used to analyze customer financial information
q.s: Kendra, a commercial loan officer, subtracts a business customer's current liabilities from its current assets to see whether it can cover its short-term debts. Kendra is calculating the customer's
q.r: Working capital. Working capital equals current assets minus current liabilities, and it shows the dollar amount a business has available to operate with after covering debts due within a year. Net income is revenue minus all expenses. Owner's equity is total assets minus total liabilities. Gross profit is sales revenue minus the cost of goods sold. None of these isolates short-term debt-paying ability.
w: Net income is revenue minus all expenses over a period, not current assets minus current liabilities.
Owner's equity is total assets minus total liabilities, while Kendra is using only the current, short-term amounts.
Gross profit is sales revenue minus the cost of goods sold, which says nothing directly about covering short-term debts.

q.pt: Describe techniques used to analyze customer financial information
q.s: An analyst at Northgate Bank restates a business client's income statement so that every expense appears as a percentage of total revenue. This technique is
q.r: Vertical analysis. Vertical analysis, also called common-size analysis, expresses each line item as a percentage of a base total within a single period; on the income statement, the base is total revenue. Horizontal analysis compares the same item across periods. Benchmarking compares a firm with industry averages or competitors. Break-even analysis finds the sales level at which total revenue equals total costs.
w: Horizontal analysis compares the same item across different periods, like this year's rent versus last year's, rather than as a percentage of revenue.
Benchmarking compares a business with industry averages or competitors, while this analyst is converting one client's own expenses into percentages of revenue.
Break-even analysis finds the sales level at which revenue equals total costs, not each expense as a percentage of revenue.

q.pt: Describe techniques used to analyze customer financial information
q.s: Data analysis at Summit Federal Bank shows that many checking customers with young children have no college savings accounts. To act on this finding, the bank should share it with its
q.r: Relationship managers and sales staff. Analyzing customer financial information often reveals cross-selling opportunities, or chances to offer current customers additional products that meet their needs. Relationship managers and sales staff work directly with customers, so they can act on these leads. The internal audit team checks controls and accuracy, data-entry processors record transactions, and regulators oversee compliance; none of them sells products to customers.
w: An internal audit and compliance team checks controls and rule-following; it does not contact customers to offer college savings accounts.
Data-entry and processing staff record transactions, so they are not in a position to offer new products to these families.
Regulators oversee whether the bank follows the law; they do not sell products, so sharing a sales opportunity with them would not help.

q.pt: Describe techniques used to analyze customer financial information
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a technique used to analyze customer financial information:
o: Updating customers' mailing addresses in the database
Printing year-end tax forms for account holders
Training tellers on a new cash-drawer procedure
Comparing profit ratios of customer accounts by region
q.r: Comparing profit ratios of customer accounts by region. Grouping customers into segments, such as regions, and comparing their profitability is a common analysis technique that shows a finance firm where its most and least profitable customers are. Updating addresses and printing tax forms are routine record-keeping tasks, not analysis. Training tellers on a cash-drawer procedure is an operations activity that does not examine customer financial data.
w: Updating mailing addresses keeps records accurate, but it is routine record-keeping that does not analyze customers' financial information.
Printing year-end tax forms is a routine reporting task, not an analysis of what customers' financial data reveals.
Training tellers on a cash-drawer procedure is an operations task that does not examine any customer's financial information.

q.pt: Describe techniques used to analyze customer financial information
q.s: A lender reviews whether Omar's monthly income is large enough to cover the payments on a new loan in addition to his existing bills. Which of the five Cs of credit is the lender evaluating?
q.r: Capacity. Capacity is the borrower's ability to repay a loan from current income after meeting other obligations, which lenders often measure with the debt-to-income ratio. Character is the borrower's trustworthiness, shown by credit history. Collateral is property pledged to secure the loan. Capital is the borrower's own money or net worth, such as savings and investments, that could be used if income falls short.
w: Character is about the borrower's trustworthiness, usually judged from credit history, not whether Omar's income can cover new payments.
Collateral is property pledged to secure the loan, not Omar's monthly income compared with the payments he owes.
Capital is the borrower's savings and net worth that could serve as a backup, while the lender is checking whether monthly income covers the payments.

q.pt: Describe techniques used to analyze customer financial information
q.s: Marcus earns $5,000 per month before taxes and pays $1,500 per month on his mortgage, car loan and credit cards. What is his debt-to-income ratio?
q.r: 30%. The debt-to-income ratio divides total monthly debt payments by gross monthly income: $1,500 ÷ $5,000 = 0.30, or 30%. Lenders use it to judge whether an applicant can handle more debt. The 70% figure is the share of income left after debt payments. The 333% figure divides income by debt instead of debt by income, and 3% misplaces the decimal point in 0.30.
w: 70% is the share of Marcus's income left after debt payments ($3,500 / $5,000), not the share that goes to debt.
This misplaces the decimal point; $1,500 / $5,000 = 0.30, which is 30%, not 3%.
This divides income by debt ($5,000 / $1,500) instead of dividing the debt payments by income.

q.pt: Describe techniques used to analyze customer financial information
q.s: A three-digit number, calculated from a person's credit report, that lenders use to predict how likely the person is to repay borrowed money is a
q.r: Credit score. A credit score summarizes the information in a credit report, such as payment history and amounts owed, into a single number that helps lenders quickly judge credit risk. A credit limit is the maximum amount a lender allows a borrower to owe. A credit report is the detailed record of accounts and payments that the score is based on. A credit line is an amount of credit available to borrow as needed.
w: A credit limit is the most a lender will let a borrower owe, which is a dollar amount, not a score predicting repayment.
A credit report is the detailed record of accounts and payments, and the three-digit number described in the question is calculated from it.
A credit line is an amount of money available to borrow as needed, not a number that predicts whether someone will repay.

q.pt: Describe techniques used to analyze customer financial information
q.s: Before applying for a mortgage, Ana obtains a document from a credit bureau that lists her open accounts, balances owed and any late payments. Ana has obtained her
q.r: Credit report. A credit report is a detailed record, compiled by a credit bureau, of a person's credit accounts, balances, payment history and public records. Lenders review it to analyze an applicant's financial behavior. A credit score is a single number calculated from the report. A bank statement lists one account's deposits and withdrawals. A loan application is the form the borrower completes to request credit.
w: A credit score is a single number calculated from the bureau's records, while Ana's document lists her accounts, balances and late payments in detail.
A bank statement comes from a bank and lists one account's deposits and withdrawals, not all of Ana's credit accounts from a credit bureau.
A loan application is the form Ana would fill out to request the mortgage, not a credit bureau's record of her accounts.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the financial-information management function
q.s: Kingsley Insurance keeps claims data in one program, payroll data in a second program and sales data in a third, and the programs cannot share information. This common financial-information management problem is known as
q.r: Data silos. Data silos occur when information is locked inside separate, task-specific software that does not connect with other systems, so managers cannot see a complete, consistent picture of the business. Data compression shrinks files for storage or transmission. Data mining searches large data sets for patterns. Data backup copies data so it can be restored after a loss. None of these describes disconnected systems.
w: Data compression shrinks files to save space or speed up transfers; it does not describe programs that cannot share information with each other.
Data mining searches large sets of data for hidden patterns, which is a use of data, not the problem of separate systems that cannot connect.
Data backup copies information so it can be restored after a loss; it does not describe claims, payroll and sales programs that cannot share data.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the financial-information management function
q.s: After Pinecrest Bank acquired Valley Savings, the two banks' customer records used different account formats and field names. What most likely caused this data problem?
o: Combining two firms with different data structures
A firewall that blocked access to customer files
Compression software that damaged the files
A shortage of storage space on bank servers
q.r: Combining two firms with different data structures. Mergers and acquisitions are a common cause of disparate data structures because each company built its systems with its own formats, codes and field names. The combined firm must map and standardize the data before it can be used reliably. A firewall controls network access, compression reduces file size, and storage shortages limit capacity; none of them changes how records are formatted.
w: A firewall controls who can reach the network, so it could block access but would not give records different formats and field names.
Compression software shrinks files, and even if it damaged them, it would not explain two banks using different account formats and field names.
A storage shortage limits how much data can be saved, but it does not cause records to use different formats and field names.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the financial-information management function
q.s: Why does the accounting department at Oakridge Wholesale monitor its accounts receivable data each week?
o: To track aging accounts and follow up on late payers
To calculate payroll taxes withheld from employees
To set selling prices for its new product lines
To schedule payments the company owes its suppliers
q.r: To track aging accounts and follow up on late payers. Accounts receivable are amounts customers owe the business. Monitoring them shows how long each balance has been outstanding, so the firm can contact slow payers early and protect its cash flow. Payroll taxes come from payroll records, prices come from pricing decisions, and payments owed to suppliers are accounts payable, not accounts receivable.
w: Payroll taxes withheld from employees come from payroll records, not from accounts receivable, which are amounts customers owe the business.
Setting prices for new products is a pricing decision, not a reason to check each week which customers still owe money.
Payments Oakridge owes its suppliers are accounts payable; accounts receivable are amounts customers owe Oakridge.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the financial-information management function
q.s: How does a financial-information system help a company prepare next year's budget?
o: It guarantees the level of next year's sales
It removes the need for managers' judgment
It shows how resources were used in past periods
It replaces the company's income statement
q.r: It shows how resources were used in past periods. A financial-information system stores historical data on revenues and spending, so managers can see where money actually went and use those patterns to set realistic future budgets. No system can guarantee future sales, and managers still apply judgment when interpreting data. The system supplies data for the income statement; it does not replace financial statements.
w: A financial-information system can show past sales trends, but future sales depend on customers and the economy, so no system can promise what next year will bring.
The system supplies the numbers, but managers still have to interpret past spending patterns and decide what the new budget should look like.
The income statement is one report built from the system's data; the question asks how the system helps with budgeting, and it does that by supplying history, not by replacing reports.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the financial-information management function
q.s: Which of the following statements about financial-information management is accurate:
o: It is the process of preparing a firm's tax returns
It is a function that outside investors perform
It means recording cash payments in a journal
It supplies data managers use for operating decisions
q.r: It supplies data managers use for operating decisions. Financial-information management collects, protects, analyzes and reports financial data so that managers throughout the business can plan, control costs and make operations decisions. Preparing tax returns and journalizing cash payments are individual accounting tasks within its scope, not the whole function. Outside investors use financial information, but the business itself manages it.
w: Preparing tax returns is only one accounting task that uses financial data, while financial-information management is the much broader job of collecting, protecting and reporting data for decisions.
Outside investors read a company's financial reports, but the company itself is the one that gathers, stores and manages that information.
Recording cash payments in a journal is a single bookkeeping step, far narrower than managing all of a firm's financial information so managers can use it.

q.pt: Explain the nature and scope of the financial-information management function
q.s: Which of the following would be considered an external user of a company's financial information:
o: A bank deciding whether to lend to the company
A department head planning next month's staffing
A sales manager reviewing regional results
A production supervisor comparing material costs
q.r: A bank deciding whether to lend to the company. External users are people and organizations outside the business, such as lenders, investors, suppliers and government agencies, who rely on its financial information to make decisions about it. A department head, a sales manager and a production supervisor all work inside the company, so they are internal users who use financial information to plan and control operations.
w: A department head planning staffing works inside the company, so this person is an internal user rather than an outside party like a lender.
A sales manager reviewing regional results is an employee using the data to run the business, which makes the manager an internal user.
A production supervisor comparing material costs is part of the company's own operations, so the supervisor uses the information internally, not as an outsider.

q.pt: Explain the role of ethics in financial-information management
q.s: The treasurer of Bright Futures Foundation makes sure donated funds are spent on programs that advance the charity's mission rather than on unnecessary costs. This is an example of
q.r: Financial stewardship. Financial stewardship is the ethical and responsible allocation of an organization's money to activities that serve its mission and the people who entrusted it with funds. Data stewardship is accountability for the accuracy, quality and proper use of an organization's data. Product stewardship is responsibility for a product's safety and environmental effects throughout its life. Environmental stewardship is responsible care of natural resources. None of these three concerns how donated funds are spent.
w: Data stewardship is about keeping information accurate and properly used, while the treasurer here is deciding how the charity's donated money gets spent.
Product stewardship deals with a product's safety and environmental effects over its life, which has nothing to do with spending donations on the charity's programs.
Environmental stewardship means caring for natural resources, but the treasurer is protecting how donors' money is used, not protecting the environment.

q.pt: Explain the role of ethics in financial-information management
q.s: To protect customers' privacy, Paulo decides which Meridian Bank employees may view or change customer account data and under what conditions. This practice is called
q.r: Access control. Access control is the practice of deciding who may view, use or change specific data and under what conditions. Limiting access protects customers' privacy and is part of a finance firm's ethical duty to safeguard the data entrusted to it. Data mining searches large data sets for patterns. Data compression reduces file size. Master data management keeps one authoritative version of key records but does not decide who may use them.
w: Data mining searches large sets of data for hidden patterns; it does not decide which Meridian Bank employees are allowed to view or change account records.
Data compression just shrinks files so they take less space, which does nothing to limit who can see customers' account data.
Master data management keeps one trusted version of key records, but Paulo's task is deciding who gets permission to see and change them.

q.pt: Explain the role of ethics in financial-information management
q.s: Which role is responsible for maintaining the accuracy, integrity and appropriate access of a specific set of a company's financial data?
q.r: Data steward. A data steward is accountable for a set of data, making sure it is accurate, consistent, properly defined and available only to authorized users. A data processor enters or handles data but is not accountable for its overall quality. An external auditor independently examines financial statements. A network administrator maintains computer networks rather than the meaning and quality of the data.
w: A data processor enters or handles data day to day but is not the person accountable for the overall accuracy and access rules of a data set.
An external auditor is an outsider who checks financial statements, not someone who maintains a company's data and controls access to it every day.
A network administrator keeps computers and connections running, but is not responsible for whether the financial data itself is accurate and properly defined.

q.pt: Explain the role of ethics in financial-information management
q.s: Talon Credit Union installs firewalls and limits which employees can view member records. These steps mainly protect members from
q.r: Identity theft. Identity theft is the use of another person's personal or financial information, without permission, to commit fraud. Because finance firms hold sensitive data, they have an ethical duty to protect it with firewalls, access limits and similar safeguards. Loan defaults are failures to repay, billing errors are accounting mistakes, and interest rates are set by market conditions; security controls do not address these.
w: A loan default happens when a borrower fails to repay, and firewalls or access limits cannot make members pay back their loans.
Billing errors are accounting mistakes, while firewalls and limited record access are meant to stop outsiders and unauthorized staff from stealing members' personal information.
Interest rates are set by market conditions, so network security and access limits at Talon Credit Union have no effect on them.

q.pt: Explain the role of ethics in financial-information management
q.s: An accounting clerk at Fairway Mortgage notices a manager changing loan records so a quarterly report will look better. What should the clerk do?
o: Ignore it because a manager approved the change
Report it through the company's ethics channels
Quietly change the records back without approval
Post a description of it on social media
q.r: Report it through the company's ethics channels. Altering records to make results look better is unethical and misleads people who rely on the reports. Reporting the problem through established channels, such as a supervisor, compliance officer or ethics hotline, protects the integrity of financial information. Ignoring it allows the misconduct to continue, changing records without authority creates new problems, and posting on social media can harm customers and the company.
w: A manager's approval does not make falsifying loan records acceptable, and staying silent lets misleading financial reports keep reaching the people who rely on them.
Secretly changing the records back means the clerk is also altering data without authority, and it leaves the misconduct hidden instead of properly investigated.
Posting about it on social media skips the company's proper channels and could expose customer information and harm the company without fixing the problem.

q.pt: Explain the role of ethics in financial-information management
q.s: Which federal law requires the chief executive and chief financial officers of public companies to certify that their firms' financial reports are accurate?
q.r: Sarbanes-Oxley Act. The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 was passed after major accounting scandals to improve the accuracy of corporate financial reporting. It requires top executives of public companies to certify their financial reports and makes them responsible for internal controls. The Fair Labor Standards Act covers wages and hours. The Truth in Lending Act requires disclosure of credit terms. The Equal Credit Opportunity Act prohibits credit discrimination.
w: The Fair Labor Standards Act sets rules for wages, overtime and work hours, not for executives certifying the accuracy of financial reports.
The Truth in Lending Act makes lenders disclose credit terms to borrowers; it does not require CEOs and CFOs to sign off on financial reports.
The Equal Credit Opportunity Act bans discrimination in lending decisions and says nothing about executives certifying their company's financial statements.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the financial-information management function
q.s: Which type of software protects a brokerage firm's computer network by blocking access by unauthorized users?
q.r: Firewall. A firewall is hardware or software that monitors network traffic and blocks unauthorized users from reaching a network, protecting sensitive financial data. Spyware is a threat, not a safeguard: it secretly gathers information about users. Compression software reduces file size for storage or transmission. Spreadsheet software organizes and calculates data but does not control network access.
w: Spyware is a threat that secretly collects information from users, so it is something a brokerage firm needs protection from, not a tool that blocks intruders.
Compression software shrinks files for storage or sending, but it does nothing to keep unauthorized users off the firm's network.
Spreadsheet software organizes and calculates numbers, but it has no role in controlling who can get into the firm's network.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the financial-information management function
q.s: Lakeshore Insurance uses one integrated system that combines its accounting, purchasing, human resources and customer data so all departments share the same master records. This system is
q.r: Enterprise resource planning (ERP). ERP software integrates a company's major processes and their data in one system, which supports master data management by keeping a single authoritative version of key records. Electronic data interchange exchanges documents between companies' computers. Customer relationship management focuses on customer contacts and sales. Point-of-sale systems record transactions at the moment of sale.
w: Electronic data interchange sends business documents like orders and invoices between different companies' computers, rather than combining one company's departments into a single system.
Customer relationship management software focuses on customer contacts and sales, so it would not tie together Lakeshore's accounting, purchasing and human resources data.
A point-of-sale system records transactions at the moment of a sale, which is far narrower than a system sharing master records across every department.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the financial-information management function
q.s: What is a key benefit of storing a company's financial data in a central data repository?
o: Each department keeps its own separate version
The company can stop using security software
Employees work from current, consistent data
Managers receive fewer reports each month
q.r: Employees work from current, consistent data. A central data repository is one shared storage location, so every user sees the same up-to-date information and reports agree with one another. Separate departmental versions are the problem a repository solves, not its benefit. A central store still needs security software because it concentrates sensitive data. The number of reports managers receive is unrelated to where the data are stored.
w: Separate departmental versions of the data are exactly the problem a central repository is designed to fix, since copies drift apart and reports stop matching.
Putting all financial data in one place actually makes security more important, because a single breach could expose everything stored there.
Where data is stored does not decide how many reports managers get; the benefit of a central repository is that everyone works from the same data.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the financial-information management function
q.s: Software that is secretly installed on a computer to gather information about the user without permission is called
q.r: Spyware. Spyware hides on a computer and collects information such as keystrokes, passwords or account numbers without the user's consent, which makes it a serious threat to financial data. A firewall is a safeguard that blocks unauthorized network access. Freeware is software offered at no cost. Compression software reduces file size. Finance firms use security software to detect and remove spyware.
w: A firewall is a safeguard that blocks unauthorized network access, which is the opposite of software that sneaks onto a computer to collect information.
Freeware simply means software offered at no cost; the term describes its price, not software that secretly installs itself to collect information about the user.
Compression software reduces file size, and it does not hide on a computer or collect information about the user.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the financial-information management function
q.s: An accountant at Westbrook CPA Group follows a suspicious payment back through each recorded entry in the accounting system to the original invoice. The accountant is using a(n)
q.r: Audit trail. An audit trail is a chronological record that links each transaction or data change to its source, so accountants and auditors can verify entries and investigate errors or fraud. Accounting software creates audit trails automatically. A firewall blocks unauthorized network users. A budget template provides a format for planning income and expenses. A compression tool reduces file size and does not trace transactions.
w: A firewall blocks unauthorized users from a network, but it does not let the accountant trace a payment back through entries to the original invoice.
A budget template is a format for planning income and expenses, not a record that links a past payment to its source documents.
A compression tool shrinks files, but it cannot show the chain of entries that connects a suspicious payment to its invoice.

q.pt: Describe the use of technology in the financial-information management function
q.s: Cedar Valley Bank wants to convert decades of older loan records stored on microfilm into searchable digital files. Which tool should it use?
q.r: Digital imaging scanner. A digital imaging scanner, such as a microfilm scanner, reads microfilm images and converts them into digital files that can be stored, indexed and searched electronically, making old records easier to retrieve and protect. Compression software can shrink files once they are digital but cannot create them. A firewall protects networks from unauthorized users. Budgeting software plans income and expenses and does not digitize records.
w: Compression software can shrink files once they are digital, but it cannot read microfilm images and turn them into digital files in the first place.
A network firewall protects the bank from unauthorized users, but it has nothing to do with converting old microfilm loan records into searchable files.
Budgeting software plans income and spending, so it would not help Cedar Valley Bank turn microfilm records into digital files.

q.pt: Demonstrate financial analysis applications
q.s: A financial analyst compares Granite Insurance's net income for 2023, 2024 and 2025 to see how much it changed from year to year. The analyst is using
q.r: Horizontal analysis. Horizontal analysis, also called trend analysis, compares the same financial statement item across two or more periods to show its dollar and percentage change over time. Vertical analysis expresses items as a percentage of a base total within one period. Benchmarking compares a firm with industry averages or competitors. Break-even analysis finds the sales level at which revenue equals total costs.
w: Vertical analysis shows each item as a percentage of a total within one period, while the analyst here is comparing net income across three different years.
Benchmarking compares a company with competitors or industry averages, but the analyst is comparing Granite Insurance only with its own past results.
Break-even analysis finds the sales level where revenue covers total costs, not how net income changed from one year to the next.

q.pt: Demonstrate financial analysis applications
q.s: Which type of financial ratio measures how efficiently a company uses its assets to generate sales?
q.r: Asset-utilization ratio. Asset-utilization, or activity, ratios such as asset turnover and inventory turnover show how much sales a firm produces from the assets it owns. Liquidity ratios measure the ability to pay short-term debts. Leverage ratios show how much of the firm is financed with debt. Market-value ratios, such as the price-earnings ratio, show how investors value the company's stock.
w: Liquidity ratios measure whether a company can pay its short-term debts, not how much in sales it gets out of its assets.
Leverage ratios show how much of a company is financed with borrowed money, which says nothing about how efficiently its assets produce sales.
Market-value ratios, like the price-earnings ratio, reflect how investors value the stock rather than how well the company uses its assets to make sales.

q.pt: Demonstrate financial analysis applications
q.s: Analysis software lets Corbin Financial compare its operating expense ratio with the average for similar firms in its industry. This feature is called
q.r: Benchmarking. Benchmarking compares a company's results or practices with a standard, such as industry averages or leading competitors, to show where it performs well or poorly. Forecasting predicts future results. Horizontal analysis compares one firm's own results across periods rather than with other firms. Budgeting creates a financial plan for a future period and compares actual results with that plan.
w: Forecasting predicts future results, but Corbin Financial is comparing its current expense ratio with what similar firms report.
Horizontal analysis compares a firm with its own earlier periods, whereas this feature compares Corbin Financial with other firms in its industry.
Budgeting sets a financial plan and compares actual results to it, not to the average results of other companies.

q.pt: Demonstrate financial analysis applications
q.s: How can an internal auditor use financial data to detect possible conflicts of interest between employees and suppliers?
o: Compare this year's revenue with last year's revenue
Calculate the company's current ratio each quarter
Cross-check employee and vendor records for matches
Review the marketing department's annual budget
q.r: Cross-check employee and vendor records for matches. Comparing employee data with vendor data, such as addresses, phone numbers or bank accounts, can reveal an employee who has a hidden interest in a supplier the company pays. Comparing revenue across years shows trends, the current ratio measures liquidity, and reviewing a department's budget shows planned spending; none of these links employees to vendors.
w: Comparing revenue across years shows whether sales are growing, but it cannot reveal a hidden link between an employee and a supplier.
The current ratio measures whether the company can pay short-term debts, so it gives the auditor no information about employees' ties to vendors.
A department's budget shows planned spending, but reviewing it would not reveal whether an employee secretly has an interest in a supplier the company pays.

q.pt: Demonstrate financial analysis applications
q.s: Finance firms use spreadsheets and databases primarily to support business decisions through
q.r: Financial analysis. Spreadsheets and databases organize large amounts of financial data and calculate ratios, trends and comparisons quickly, so managers can evaluate performance and make decisions. They can also hold other kinds of data, but their main financial use is analysis. Market research studies customers and markets, employee training develops workers' skills, and product design creates new goods or services.
w: Market research studies customers and markets, which is not the main way finance firms use spreadsheets and databases to support decisions.
Employee training builds workers' skills, while spreadsheets and databases in finance mainly crunch financial data into ratios, trends and comparisons.
Product design is about creating new goods or services, not the number-crunching that finance firms mainly use spreadsheets and databases for.

q.pt: Demonstrate financial analysis applications
q.s: Ashford Bank's loan revenue grew from $2,400,000 in 2025 to $2,700,000 in 2026. Using horizontal analysis, what is the percentage change?
q.r: 12.5%. Horizontal analysis divides the dollar change by the earlier, or base, year: ($2,700,000 − $2,400,000) ÷ $2,400,000 = 0.125, or 12.5%. The 11.1% figure wrongly divides by the later year. The 112.5% figure shows 2026 revenue as a percentage of 2025 revenue rather than the change. The 88.9% figure divides the earlier year by the later year.
w: This figure comes from dividing the $300,000 increase by the 2026 amount instead of the 2025 base year, which is the year horizontal analysis measures from.
This figure is 2026 revenue divided by 2025 revenue, which shows the new year as a percentage of the old one rather than the change.
This figure divides the 2025 revenue by the 2026 revenue, flipping the years and never measuring the $300,000 increase at all.

q.pt: Demonstrate financial analysis applications
q.s: Which of the following is a leverage ratio:
q.r: Debt-to-equity ratio. Leverage ratios measure how much of a company is financed with borrowed money; the debt-to-equity ratio divides total liabilities by owners' equity. The acid-test ratio is a liquidity ratio that measures the ability to pay short-term debts without selling inventory. Asset turnover is an asset-utilization ratio. Net profit margin is a profitability ratio showing profit per dollar of sales.
w: The acid-test ratio is a liquidity ratio that checks whether a company can pay short-term debts without selling inventory, not how much debt finances it.
Asset turnover is an asset-utilization ratio showing how efficiently assets produce sales, so it does not measure borrowing the way a leverage ratio does.
Net profit margin is a profitability ratio showing profit per dollar of sales, not how much of the company is financed with debt.

q.pt: Demonstrate budgeting applications
q.s: Tasha owns a small tax-preparation firm and wants the easiest way to organize her income and expense data before building next year's budget. What should she do?
o: Write each figure in a paper ledger
Enter the data into budgeting software
Wait until the end of next year
q.r: Enter the data into budgeting software. Budgeting software sorts income and expenses into categories, totals them automatically and reduces calculation errors, which makes it the easiest way to organize data for a budget. A paper ledger is slow and harder to analyze. Estimating from memory produces unreliable figures. Waiting until the end of next year defeats the purpose of planning in advance.
w: A paper ledger can record the figures, but adding, sorting and analyzing them by hand is slow and error-prone, so it is not the easiest option for Tasha.
Estimating from memory would give Tasha unreliable numbers, which defeats the purpose of organizing real income and expense data for a budget.
Waiting until the end of next year means the budget would come too late to guide spending, when the point is to plan ahead.

q.pt: Demonstrate budgeting applications
q.s: A key benefit of budgeting software is that it allows users to
o: guarantee that actual spending will match planned spending.
skip recording actual income and expenses.
run what-if scenarios to see how changes affect the budget.
avoid setting financial goals for the period.
q.r: Run what-if scenarios to see how changes affect the budget. What-if analysis lets a user change one assumption, such as sales volume or an interest rate, and instantly see the effect on the entire budget, which supports better planning. Software cannot guarantee that actual results will match the plan. Users must still record actual income and expenses, and setting goals remains the starting point of any budget.
w: Budgeting software helps plan and track spending, but nothing can force actual spending to match the plan, since real costs and income still change.
Users still have to record actual income and expenses, because the software can only compare plans with reality if that real data is entered.
Setting financial goals is still the starting point of any budget, and the software helps reach those goals rather than removing the need for them.

q.pt: Demonstrate budgeting applications
q.s: Ravi's budgeting app connects to his bank and credit card accounts and places each purchase into the correct spending category without manual entry. This feature is called
q.r: Automatic tracking. Automatic tracking links budgeting software to financial accounts and imports transactions into budget categories, saving time and reducing data-entry errors. Automatic alerts send notices when spending nears a limit or a bill is due. What-if analysis tests how changed assumptions affect the budget. Variance analysis compares actual results with budgeted amounts after transactions are recorded.
w: Automatic alerts send warnings, such as when spending nears a limit, but they do not pull in Ravi's purchases and sort them into categories.
What-if analysis tests how changing an assumption affects a budget, while Ravi's app is simply importing and sorting real purchases.
Variance analysis compares actual spending with the budget afterward, but the feature described is the one that collects and categorizes the purchases in the first place.

q.pt: Demonstrate budgeting applications
q.s: Cora receives a text message from her budgeting software when her restaurant spending reaches 90% of its monthly limit. Which feature sent the message?
q.r: Automatic alerts. Automatic alerts notify users when spending approaches or exceeds a budget limit, when a balance is low or when a bill is due, so they can adjust before a problem grows. Automatic tracking imports transactions into categories but does not warn the user. Budget templates provide a ready-made format for building a budget. Data compression reduces file size.
w: Automatic tracking imports and sorts Cora's purchases into categories, but it is not the feature that sends her a warning when she nears a limit.
Budget templates give a ready-made layout for building a budget, and they do not send messages when spending gets close to a limit.
Data compression shrinks file sizes, so it has nothing to do with texting Cora about her restaurant spending.

q.pt: Demonstrate budgeting applications
q.s: Managing budget data efficiently with budgeting tools gives a business owner
o: a guarantee of higher annual profits.
an exemption from paying business taxes.
q.r: More confidence in budget decisions. When budget data are organized, accurate and current, an owner can trust the numbers and make spending and saving decisions with greater confidence. Good budget management improves planning, but it cannot guarantee profits. Expenses must still be tracked for the budget to be useful, and budgeting has no effect on a business's legal duty to pay taxes.
w: Well-managed budget data improves planning, but profits still depend on sales, costs and the market, so no budgeting tool can guarantee them.
Budgeting tools only work when daily expenses are recorded, so good budget management depends on tracking rather than freeing the owner from it.
Budgeting has no effect on tax law, so organizing budget data does not excuse a business from paying the taxes it owes.

q.pt: Demonstrate budgeting applications
q.s: After the quarter ends, the finance manager at Elm Street Credit Union uses budgeting software to compare actual expenses with the amounts that were planned. This comparison is called
q.r: Variance analysis. Variance analysis compares actual results with budgeted amounts to find differences, or variances, so managers can learn why spending was higher or lower than planned and take action. Horizontal analysis compares financial statement items across periods. Forecasting predicts future results. Benchmarking compares a firm's performance with that of other companies or industry averages.
w: Horizontal analysis compares the same item across different periods, while the finance manager is comparing actual expenses with the planned amounts for one quarter.
Forecasting predicts future results, but this manager is looking back at a finished quarter to see how actual spending differed from the plan.
Benchmarking compares a firm with other companies or industry averages, whereas Elm Street Credit Union is comparing its actual results with its own budget.

q.pt: Discuss non-traditional uses for financial information (e.g., lean, sustainability reporting, activity-based costing [ABC], six sigma)
q.s: Westfield Mortgage maps its loan-approval process and removes steps that add no value for borrowers, such as entering the same data twice. Westfield is applying
q.r: Lean. Lean is an approach that improves efficiency by identifying and eliminating waste, meaning any step or activity that does not add value for the customer. Six Sigma uses statistical data to reduce defects and variation. Activity-based costing assigns overhead costs according to the activities that cause them. Sustainability reporting discloses a company's environmental and social performance.
w: Six Sigma uses statistics to cut errors and variation, while Westfield is mapping its process to remove steps like double data entry that add no value.
Activity-based costing assigns overhead costs to products by the activities that cause them; it does not remove wasteful steps from a process.
Sustainability reporting shares environmental and social results with stakeholders, which is not what Westfield is doing when it trims its loan-approval steps.

q.pt: Discuss non-traditional uses for financial information (e.g., lean, sustainability reporting, activity-based costing [ABC], six sigma)
q.s: What is a benefit of applying Six Sigma to a bank's financial processes?
o: Overhead is assigned to products by activity
Environmental results are reported to stakeholders
Loan decisions are made without using data
Problems are identified and inefficiencies are reduced
q.r: Problems are identified and inefficiencies are reduced. Six Sigma is a data-driven quality-improvement method that measures a process, finds the causes of errors and variation, and removes them, which leads to fewer mistakes and lower costs. Assigning overhead by activity describes activity-based costing. Reporting environmental results describes sustainability reporting. Six Sigma depends on data rather than replacing it.
w: Assigning overhead to products by activity describes activity-based costing, a different method from Six Sigma's focus on finding and removing errors.
Reporting environmental results to stakeholders is sustainability reporting, not the quality-improvement work Six Sigma brings to a bank's processes.
Six Sigma depends heavily on data to measure processes and find causes of errors, so it would never mean making loan decisions without data.

q.pt: Discuss non-traditional uses for financial information (e.g., lean, sustainability reporting, activity-based costing [ABC], six sigma)
q.s: Driftwood Insurance assigns its overhead costs to each type of policy based on the number of claims processed and customer calls handled for that type. This costing method is
q.r: Activity-based costing. Activity-based costing (ABC) assigns overhead to products or services according to the activities, or cost drivers, that consume resources, such as claims processed or calls handled. This gives a more accurate picture of what each product really costs. Lean eliminates waste, Six Sigma reduces defects and variation, and sustainability reporting discloses environmental and social performance.
w: Lean focuses on removing wasteful steps from a process, not on dividing overhead costs among policy types based on claims and calls.
Six Sigma reduces defects and variation using statistics, while Driftwood is deciding how to split overhead costs among its policy types.
Sustainability reporting discloses environmental and social performance, not how overhead is assigned based on claims processed and calls handled.

q.pt: Discuss non-traditional uses for financial information (e.g., lean, sustainability reporting, activity-based costing [ABC], six sigma)
q.s: Ferris Bank tracks the energy and paper costs of its branches and publishes the results, along with its goals for reducing waste, for customers and investors. This practice is
q.r: Sustainability reporting. Sustainability reporting uses financial and operating data to disclose a company's environmental, social and economic performance, such as energy use and waste, to stakeholders. Activity-based costing assigns overhead to products by activity. Horizontal analysis compares financial statement items across periods. Six Sigma is a quality-improvement method that reduces defects and variation.
w: Activity-based costing assigns overhead to products by activity, while Ferris Bank is publicly sharing its energy and paper use and its waste-reduction goals.
Horizontal analysis compares financial statement items across periods, but Ferris Bank's practice is publishing environmental results and goals for customers and investors.
Six Sigma is a method for reducing errors in processes, not a way of reporting energy use and waste goals to stakeholders.

q.pt: Discuss employment opportunities in the finance industry
q.s: Darnell works for Midway Savings Bank, where he studies each small business's financial statements, cash flow and credit history and then recommends whether the bank should approve its loan request. Darnell is most likely a(n)
q.r: Credit analyst. A credit analyst evaluates the financial condition and credit history of people or businesses that apply for loans and judges how likely they are to repay. The analyst's recommendation helps the lender decide whether to approve the loan and on what terms. An actuary uses statistics to measure risk for insurers, an insurance agent sells insurance policies, and a bank teller handles routine deposits and withdrawals.
w: An actuary uses statistics to measure risk for insurance companies, while Darnell reviews business finances to recommend whether a bank should approve loans.
An insurance agent sells insurance policies to customers, which is very different from analyzing a business's credit history and cash flow for a loan decision.
A bank teller handles routine deposits and withdrawals, not in-depth reviews of financial statements to judge whether a business will repay a loan.

q.pt: Discuss employment opportunities in the finance industry
q.s: Elena meets with first-time home buyers, explains the differences among several home loan options, and helps each buyer complete a loan application. Elena's job title is most likely
q.r: Mortgage loan officer. A mortgage loan officer works for a lender and guides customers through choosing and applying for a loan to buy a home. Because a home loan is a large, long-term commitment, the loan officer explains options and helps buyers gather the required information. A claims adjuster investigates insurance claims, a controller oversees a company's accounting, and a compliance analyst checks that a firm follows laws and regulations.
w: A claims adjuster investigates insurance claims after a loss, while Elena works with home buyers to choose and apply for home loans.
A controller oversees a company's internal accounting, not meeting with home buyers to explain loan options.
A compliance analyst checks that a firm follows laws and regulations, rather than guiding first-time buyers through home loan applications.

q.pt: Discuss employment opportunities in the finance industry
q.s: Which finance professional is primarily responsible for recording, analyzing and reporting a company's financial transactions?
q.r: Accountant. Accountants record financial transactions, analyze the results and prepare reports such as financial statements so that owners, managers, lenders and governments can make decisions. Accounting is one of the largest career areas in the finance industry. An underwriter evaluates risk to decide whether to insure or lend, a stockbroker buys and sells securities for clients, and a loan officer helps customers obtain loans.
w: An underwriter evaluates risk to decide whether to insure or lend, rather than recording and reporting all of a company's transactions.
A stockbroker buys and sells securities for clients, which is not the same as recording and reporting a company's financial transactions.
A loan officer helps customers get loans, but does not keep and report a company's own financial records.

q.pt: Discuss employment opportunities in the finance industry
q.s: Tomas wants a finance career in which he helps individuals and families create budgets, save for retirement and choose the right insurance. Tomas is most interested in the area of
q.r: Personal finance. Personal finance is the area of finance that serves individuals and households, helping them budget, save, borrow, invest and protect themselves with insurance. Financial planners and personal financial advisors work in this area. Corporate finance manages money for businesses, public finance manages money for government agencies, and international finance deals with money flows between countries, so none of these focus on individual families.
w: Corporate finance manages money for businesses, while Tomas wants to help individuals and families with budgets, retirement and insurance.
Public finance deals with money for government agencies, not with helping households budget and save for retirement.
International finance covers money flows between countries, which has little to do with helping a family build a budget or pick insurance.

q.pt: Discuss employment opportunities in the finance industry
q.s: Which of the following is an example of a task performed by a finance professional:
o: Planning the menu for a hotel banquet
Examining accounting records for signs of fraud
Creating social media posts for a retailer
q.r: Examining accounting records for signs of fraud. Examining accounting records for signs of fraud is finance work often done by forensic accountants, auditors and fraud investigators. These professionals trace transactions, spot irregularities and help protect organizations and their stakeholders from financial loss. Planning a banquet menu belongs to hospitality, creating social media posts belongs to marketing, and repairing a computer network belongs to information technology.
w: Planning a banquet menu is hospitality work, since it involves food and events rather than money, records or financial decisions.
Creating social media posts for a retailer is marketing work, not a task that involves analyzing or protecting financial information.
Repairing a computer network is information technology work, even if a finance firm owns the network, because it does not involve handling money or financial records.

q.pt: Discuss employment opportunities in the finance industry
q.s: Which statement about the skills needed for a career in finance is most accurate?
o: Math ability is the main skill that employers look for.
Interpersonal skills are important mainly for sales positions.
Soft skills such as communication and teamwork are highly valued.
Speed in completing tasks matters more than ethical judgment.
q.r: Soft skills such as communication and teamwork are highly valued. Finance professionals need technical knowledge, but they also work with clients, coworkers and regulators, and their work depends on trust. Employers therefore value soft skills such as listening, explaining complex information clearly, working on teams and acting ethically. Math skills alone are not enough, interpersonal skills matter in every finance role rather than mainly in sales, and speed never outweighs ethical judgment in handling other people's money.
w: Math ability helps in finance, but employers also need people who can communicate with clients, work in teams and act ethically, so math alone is not the main thing.
Interpersonal skills matter in every finance role, since analysts, accountants and advisors all work with coworkers and clients, not only salespeople.
Finance professionals handle other people's money, so ethical judgment is essential and can never take a back seat to finishing tasks quickly.

q.pt: Discuss employment opportunities in the finance industry
q.s: Haruto works for an insurance company, where he uses statistics and probability to estimate how likely policyholders are to file claims so the company can set premium rates. Haruto is a(n)
q.r: Actuary. An actuary uses mathematics, statistics and probability to measure the financial cost of risk. Insurance companies rely on actuaries to estimate future claims and to help set premiums that cover those claims and keep the company financially sound. A bank teller handles routine customer transactions, a loan officer helps customers obtain loans, and a financial planner advises individuals on reaching personal financial goals.
w: A bank teller handles routine deposits and withdrawals, not statistical estimates of how often policyholders will file claims.
A loan officer helps customers apply for loans, while Haruto uses probability to help an insurer set premiums.
A financial planner advises individuals on personal goals like retirement, rather than calculating claim risk so an insurance company can price its policies.

q.pt: Discuss employment opportunities in the finance industry
q.s: Kiara's job at Brightwater Bank includes opening checking accounts for customers, explaining savings options and helping them apply for debit cards. Kiara works in which area of the finance industry?
q.r: Banking services. Banking services include accepting deposits, opening checking and savings accounts, providing debit cards, making loans and processing payments for customers. Positions such as personal banker and teller are common entry points into this area of finance. Insurance protects against financial loss, securities and investments involve buying and selling stocks and bonds, and public accounting firms provide audit, tax and accounting services to clients.
w: Insurance protects people and businesses against financial loss, while Kiara is opening checking accounts and issuing debit cards for bank customers.
Securities and investments involve buying and selling stocks and bonds, not opening checking accounts or explaining savings options.
Public accounting firms provide audit, tax and accounting services to clients, which is different from Kiara's work opening accounts at a bank.

q.pt: Discuss opportunities for building professional relationships in finance
q.s: At a neighbor's backyard barbecue, Marcus, a financial advisor, chats with a local tax accountant, and the two agree to meet next week to discuss referring clients to each other. Marcus is networking at a
q.r: Social gathering. Networking does not happen only at business events; informal settings such as parties, barbecues and community events often lead to valuable professional relationships. Marcus made a business contact in a relaxed, social setting and followed up with a plan to share referrals. A trade show and a professional conference are formal business events, and a board meeting is a governance meeting rather than a networking setting.
w: A trade show is a formal business event where companies display products, but Marcus met the accountant at a neighbor's backyard barbecue.
A board meeting is where directors govern an organization, not a casual setting like the barbecue where Marcus made the new contact.
Networking does happen at professional conferences, but this contact was made at a neighbor's barbecue, which is an informal social event.

q.pt: Discuss opportunities for building professional relationships in finance
q.s: Jada, a new financial planner, wants to build long-term relationships with more clients. Which of the following is the most effective way for her to do this:
o: Encourage satisfied clients to refer friends and colleagues
Send the same promotional email to purchased contact lists
Offer her services to close friends and family members
Limit follow-up contact so clients do not feel pressured
q.r: Encourage satisfied clients to refer friends and colleagues. A referral system builds a client base on trust, because new prospects arrive with a recommendation from someone they already know. Satisfied clients who refer friends also deepen their own relationship with the planner. Mass emails to strangers seldom build relationships, serving friends and family limits growth, and limiting follow-up weakens the contact that relationships need.
w: Sending the same email to purchased lists reaches strangers who did not ask to hear from Jada, which rarely builds trust or long-term relationships.
Friends and family may become early clients, but that small circle limits how many new long-term relationships Jada can build.
Relationships need regular contact to grow, so cutting back on follow-up would weaken the client connections Jada is trying to strengthen.

q.pt: Discuss opportunities for building professional relationships in finance
q.s: Strong professional relationships in finance are usually __________, with both parties sharing information, advice and opportunities over time.
q.r: Reciprocal. A reciprocal relationship is one in which both people give and receive benefits. In finance, professionals who share leads, advice and referrals with their contacts receive the same support in return, which makes the relationship last. One-sided relationships, in which one person only takes, fade quickly, temporary contacts do not build trust, and treating every contact as a competitor discourages the sharing that networking depends on.
w: A one-sided relationship, where only one person benefits, does not involve both parties sharing information and opportunities, so it tends to fade quickly.
Temporary contacts end before trust can develop, while the question describes relationships where both sides keep sharing over time.
Some competition exists in finance, but treating contacts as rivals discourages the open sharing of advice and opportunities that strong relationships depend on.

q.pt: Discuss opportunities for building professional relationships in finance
q.s: Which activity would most likely help a young accountant build lasting relationships with other professionals in the field:
o: Serving on a committee of a professional accounting association
Attending one industry event without speaking to anyone
Following accounting leaders online without interacting
Collecting business cards at events without following up
q.r: Serving on a committee of a professional accounting association. Taking an active role in a professional association, such as serving on a committee or helping plan events, gives members repeated, meaningful contact with others in their field. Working together on shared goals builds trust and lasting relationships. Attending without speaking, following people online without interacting, and collecting cards without follow-up are passive activities that create contacts but rarely relationships.
w: Showing up to one event without talking to anyone gives the accountant no real contact with others, so no relationship can form.
Following leaders online without interacting is passive, so those leaders never get to know the accountant and no lasting relationship develops.
Collecting business cards is a start, but without follow-up those contacts are quickly forgotten and never turn into lasting relationships.

q.pt: Discuss opportunities for building professional relationships in finance
q.s: Priya, a new analyst at a regional bank, wants an experienced colleague who will give her career advice and introduce her to other professionals in the industry. Priya should look for a(n)
q.r: Mentor. A mentor is an experienced professional who guides a less experienced person, offering career advice and often introducing the mentee to useful contacts. Mentoring relationships help new finance professionals learn how the industry works and build their professional networks more quickly. A trustee manages property for the benefit of others, an underwriter evaluates risk to decide whether to insure or lend, and an auditor examines financial records and controls.
w: A trustee manages property or money on behalf of others, not an experienced colleague who gives Priya career advice and introductions.
An underwriter evaluates risk to decide whether to insure or lend, which is a job role rather than a guiding relationship for a new analyst.
An auditor examines financial records and controls, not a person whose role is to coach Priya and introduce her to industry contacts.

q.pt: Discuss opportunities for building professional relationships in finance
q.s: The office manager at Halvorsen Insurance wants to strengthen the agency's relationship with the vendor that handles its payroll. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Offer the representative a personal cash gift for lower prices
Contact the vendor mainly when payroll problems arise
Ask the vendor about other clients' payroll details
Invite the vendor's representative to a casual business lunch
q.r: Invite the vendor's representative to a casual business lunch. A casual shared activity, such as a business lunch, lets both parties get to know each other and builds goodwill in an ethical way. Strong vendor relationships lead to better service and smoother problem-solving. A personal cash gift to win lower prices is a bribe, contacting the vendor mainly when problems occur keeps the relationship negative, and asking for other clients' details pressures the vendor to break confidentiality.
w: A personal cash gift meant to win lower prices is a bribe, which is unethical and would damage trust rather than build a healthy vendor relationship.
Reaching out only when payroll problems happen keeps every contact negative, which does little to strengthen the relationship with the vendor.
Asking for other clients' payroll details pressures the vendor to break confidentiality, which would harm trust instead of building it.

q.pt: Discuss opportunities for building professional relationships in finance
q.s: Why do many financial advisors build relationships with professionals outside their own specialty, such as attorneys and real estate agents?
o: To replace the need for professional licenses
To exchange referrals and expertise that benefit clients
To share client information without permission
To limit the number of competitors in the market
q.r: To exchange referrals and expertise that benefit clients. Clients often need help that crosses specialties, such as estate planning, taxes or buying a home. By building relationships with attorneys, accountants and real estate agents, advisors can refer clients to trusted experts and receive referrals in return. Relationships do not replace licenses, sharing client information without permission breaks confidentiality, and limiting competitors is not a legitimate purpose of networking.
w: Professional relationships do not replace licenses, since advisors still must meet licensing rules no matter whom they know.
